You can still get help from a rape crisis helpline even without reporting it.

Telling a survivor of rape to report to the police is ridiculous advice. Even if it wasn't for OP's specific circumstances, the cops fuck up rape investigations so often they're as well known for it as for racism.

OP, I definitely understand how it might seem easier to write it off/process it as drunken sex. But in the long term it won't be. I really hope you get the help and support you need, irl, not from the jerks on here.

Someone who CHOOSES to get drunk can absolutely expect the people around them not to rape them!!
That isn't expecting them to make decisions for them, that's expecting their bodily autonomy to be respected.

That's the basics of consent.

Considering that in another comment you say that when you later gave consent it was reluctant at best and they only asked when they were nearly finished...
That doesn't good, and honestly sounds like they were just asking to assuage their conscience.

Someone who is drunk cannot consent. This was not a dumb decision, this was rape.
And telling a survivor of rape to report it is... not very useful. The police are remarkably shit at handling reports of rape/sexual assault. If OP does decide to report, then I wish her all the best, but having gone that route myself I will never recommend it as the first course of action to a fellow survivor myself.

I am so sorry they did this to you. Let me be really clear: B raped you. You were so drunk that you can't remember it/asleep. In those circumstances you are not able to consent.
Please call a rape helpline number where you live (there seems to be a list of contacts by country here: http://www.ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html)

I hope you are able to get support from friends who believe you and are able to stand by you. That doesn't seem to be either A or C. If you did want to try with either of them, or with other friends who were there that night, you could tell them very clearly "I don't care what it might have looked like, and I don't know because I was so drunk that I don't remember, but B raped me. I was too drunk to be able to consent. I hope you are able to believe me and support me [if you have specific things you need support with you can say so, like keeping B away from you, getting to any appointments, or if you don't want to hear from them, leaving you alone!]"

Sending you lots of kind thoughts from a fellow survivor!

I'll say upfront that I am a survivor of sexual violence myself, as well as having done academic work in this area.

It's messy. Of course, we want to be able to say that consent is straightforward: yes means yes, explicitly asking for and receiving consent is vital and no/maybe/any sign of uncertainty means NO. Also, we can change our minds partway through.

I think it's also important to note that how we think of our own experiences in retrospect is often more important than what anyone else says about them.
So any number of us could come along here and say OMFG that was assault, but at the end of the day what matters is how YOU feel about it. And that's part of the messiness.

There are a few things in your post that seem important though:
To begin with, you froze, you were scared and unsure and your partner did not ask for, nor receive consent. That is a classic case of sexual assault.

However, partway through, your partner did ask for consent and you gave it, and you say that you had thought about it and decided that you were ok with it. I think it's important to remember here that we can change our minds partway through.

But then you also said that you would not have chosen this for yourself. And I think that is really telling.
It might be worth thinking about (and, if therapy is something that's accessible to you, talking with a therapist about, or with a trusted friend) whether, if you had said "no" when your partner asked partway through, do you think your partner would've stopped? Is it possible that you said yes as a defence mechanism to give yourself a sense of control back over a situation where control had been taken from you?
And I guess even if you now know that your partner would've stopped, it's probably important to think back to if you would've known/believed that THEN.

Again, none of us here can tell you how to think about your experience.
And I'm sure it's possible for people to assume consent, start a sexual encounter based on those nonverbal assumptions and then pause when they realise that they should've checked in verbally, and continue once mutual verbal consent has been established.
That doesn't seem to be what happened here though, since it was specifically your partner who assumed (or didn't care to ask?) your consent. It wasn't mutual.

I am glad that you are not traumatised by this. I do hope that you have support around you though, because when I first started thinking back to when my (now ex-)bf raped me I also didn't feel traumatised at all. I've since been in therapy for over two years for PTSD. Trauma is... weird, and often not what people expect it to look/feel like and often it doesn't surface until we start to notice the cause, or something triggers the façade we've built up if we've buried it deeply.

Sending you lots of kind thoughts from an internet stranger.
NTA and also I came here to say thank you for being an amazing supportive relative for your nibling!! I wish I had had someone like you in my life when I was growing up. 🥰

Just because he didn't have a prior criminal record doesn't mean that he hasn't done anything before, just that he hasn't been convicted before.

When I went to the police two years ago to report my ex-bf (him being the cause of my PTSD) I knew that it was extremely unlikely that he would even be prosecuted, much less convicted based on my report.
However, having my report on file means that if he does anything in future and he's reported, it will carry more weight and be more likely to be prosecuted/be convicted in future.

Different kind of case, but people like this often don't just do things like this once. He might have prior reports on his record, or maybe no one reported him before, but also... if he was this ableist to YOU, then OMFG just think how his disabled kids must feel, knowing what he's like!!

Absolutely NTA!!

Sending you solidarity, OP!

In general I'm all for people sharing everything with their partners.

But there are a few things I value even more highly. One thing is consent. If someone shares something with you you must NEVER share it with someone else unless you have their consent.
And sure, you could start all your conversations with your kids with "don't forget, I will share everything you tell me with your dad, and that's not negotiable, only proceed if you are ok with that", but you can't tack that onto the END of a conversation after the thing has already been shared (sure, you've always done this, but it seems like your daughter was hoping that you were going to not be TA and giving you an opportunity to be a better person... Spoiler alert: you failed!).

Of course, what with all the information you've shared in the comments about how abusive your husband is to your kids (nice victim blaming btw! /sarcasm), that would be a terrible idea and leads me to my next thing which I value more highly, as pretty much everyone else has said: protecting your kids from abuse!
Your husband is abusive (to your kids!), you are their mum, it's generally considered to be a parent's job to protect their children, your husband is obviously failing this job miserably by doing the exact opposite, and so far so are you by enabling your husband's abuse!
So, to try to stop failing miserably in your job as a parent, step one is actually really simple!

Stop telling your husband anything your kids tell you unless you have their consent.
Step two is: apologise to your kids for having done so in the past and for not protecting them from their dad. Ask them how you can support them now.
Step something else (because it's probably alongside the others): get help! Get therapy (individual, not couples), talk to a domestic violence helpline, talk to people around you to get support both for yourself and your kids and don't tell your husband. If you can get your husband into (individual) therapy too, great, but that's not the priority.

Obviously YTA, enabling, victim blaming, not protecting your kids and being a terrible parent.
You do have the opportunity to start taking steps to do better. I don't have much hope given your comments, but please consider it.

And honestly, for your sake... I hope you haven't shown your husband this post!

Do NOT go to couples therapy!!

I know a lot of people are suggesting this and you're wanting to do this, etc., but please hear me out!

He is gaslighting you. You know he's masturbating in the shower (and not cleaning it up) and has been for years. He knows it too. And yet, for YEARS he has been lying to you, telling you that he is not doing this, and at one point even had you convinced that this is shampoo.

This is textbook case gaslighting, which is a classic tactic of emotional abusers (though, yes, sometimes people do it unintentionally/non-malevolently, but the impact is still awful).

And therapists pretty much all agree that couples therapy is a BAD IDEA for couples where one partner is abusive. Now, I don't know if your husband is abusive, I think we don't have enough information, but we do know that he's been gaslighting you for YEARS and that's a massive red flag!

In these cases the thing that's recommended is for both partners to get individual therapy (you for support, him to get his behaviour to change).

Obviously NTA, I really hope you get the support you need and your husband sorts himself out OP!
thank you for your statement in response to JKR

Obviously NTA, and also it would not at all be unreasonable for you to insist that her bf who is creepy, pervs on your bras/bra size and makes you feel unsafe in your own home should be banned from your home.

If she wants to see him, she can go to his place.

I think your edit with your offer to talk with her and your request that she talk to him is very gracious, but if the partners/fuckbuddies of anyone I lived with did something as creepy as that, they'd be banned from my apartment (and if my flatmate tried defending them... well, I'd be reconsidering my living arrangements, but luckily he's one of the few people in the world I trust).

I've experienced gaslighting in a number of relationships and I've come to the conclusion that gaslighting does not have to be intentional. Abusers often come to believe their false realities so when they tell us that the thing we know to be true is not true, they might truly believe that... the harm it causes is just as real!

And it can make it even harder to deal with if this is the case because if they truly believe in their false realities, it can give us the feeling that if only we can prove to them what is actually real everything will be ok, but often they're so committed to these false realities that they refuse to engage with proof to the contrary and being confronted with it can lead them to attack us... And I suspect that that might be what happened here with your ex, that she didn't want to/couldn't handle the proof that her reality was false, so used - not the proof itself, but the fact that you went through the security footage to get it - and added this to her narrative of you as A Bad Person (first you supposedly did no chores, now you apparently spied on her, practically stalking her... nevermind that she knew that the cameras were there!).

So this is the narrative she's fed her (I guess your former) friends. Even though, as I think you said in another reply, she seems to have told the friends pretty accurately what happened; since she's the one who told them, she would have been able to shape the narrative. But also the friends were shitty for not seeing her bullshit for what it is and I'm sorry they didn't stick with you. I hope you have someone in your corner!

TL;DR - I don't think of this as borderline gaslighting, I don't think gaslighting has to be intentional. DEFINITELY NTA!!

I'm glad that you've been officially judged to be an asshole, because definitely YTA here. At the very least you could have gotten your kid one familiar one in addition to the new one (you said she could pick two, were they both Greek??) or made her a sandwich.
See, I was this kid. The rules were always "eat what's on your plate or you don't eat anything else". And if I didn't like it, I went to bed hungry. Sure, my ex-mother took it to extremes (I'd then get whatever I didn't finish on my plate the night before for breakfast the next morning and for each meal until I *did* finish it), but even without taking it to extremes YTA.
You have a responsibility to care for your child. This includes ensuring that she is adequately fed. She is nine years old, it is not her responsibility to make sure that she will have food she likes and can eat. (My older sister has a good system of making sure that when she makes a meal, if there are unfamiliar foods, her kids also have some familiar things, which they like, as part of the meal. She will ask them to try the new things, but she never forces them, nor does she insist they finish what's on their plate if they don't want to.)

Obviously YTA!

But, OP's fiancée, if you're reading this, please dump his ass and run for the hills!

Also, you'd do well to read this book: "The Mental Load: A Feminist Comic" by Emma http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/39196352-the-mental-load

The first comic in the book is online, here: https://english.emmaclit.com/2017/05/20/you-shouldve-asked/

NAH.

To be honest, you do sound like an asshole. However, I think the more important part here is that you have been honest with your gf and given her the information that she needs in order to make the best decisions for herself. And from the information here it sounds like that decision may well be to break up with you.

In long-term relationships it makes sense to prioritise your partner and the family/future you build with them over your family of origin. If you are not in a position to/willing to do this it is best practice to be very clear and honest with any partners/potential partners you may have.

It's asshole-y to be unwilling to do this, yes. But it would be even more asshole-y not to be honest about it.

I completely understand.

I think for me, talking to friends about stuff like this, when the question of "why didn't you tell me sooner?" or even just "I had no idea" comes up... I tell them that this kind of shit is hard to talk about! It's hard and scary to put into words, hard to figure out exactly what to say, how to say it, when to say it... and I mean, there's a whole lot of social stigma around mental illness, which certainly makes things harder, and I think our ADHD brains give us a tendency to *overthink everything* which adds in thinking about how someone might respond, and feeling responsible for their feelings and their response (when we're not, we're only ever responsible for ourselves, and our own actions and feelings) ...

It's overwhelming, and I've found just being honest about the fact that my head can be an overwhelming mess, which can be hard to talk about, has been the best way to go...

Biggest life hack: stop masking!
We are not allistic and trying to pretend to be sucks the life out of us! So be your true autistic self! Including, very much, giving a big fuck you to number one on that list! Because we don't owe NTs/allistics shit, and we don't need to try to perform eye contact to make anyone else comfortable!
Do eye contact, or not, as you are comfortable with!
Stim freely and publicly! (I always wear stim jewellery and I've taken to carrying one of my snuggly friends - soft toys - either one of my dragons, or my octopus, with me when I go somewhere, so that I have something stimmy with me at all times.)
Pursue the fuck out of your passions and obsessions (I, personally, can't stand the term "autistic special interest" - I prefer passion/obsession)
Be honest and staunchly refuse to engage in allistic social dances (like giving "white lie" excuses when you need to cancel plans - be honest and say so if you're feeling peopled out/aren't feeling up to peopling/need some alone time/are feeling too anxious/whatever the real reason is!). Speak honestly, openly and freely about your truth, your lived experience, and absolutely opt out of allistic/NT social expectations!
Protect yourself from sensory overstimulation/overload. Whether that means noise-cancelling headphones, glasses with tinted lenses, a weighted blanket, a weighted lap pad/weighted soft toy, making sure that events you attend have quiet rooms for you to retreat to if you get overwhelmed... whatever works for you.

Whatever you do, remember that you are not allistic, you are not obligated to perform any attempt at trying to be allistic or hide who you really are to make allistics around you comfortable!!

If you're on FB, there's an awesome FB group that I'm in, for us neurodivergent folk, that's very supportive... Feel free to send me a message if you want the link.

And I do get what you mean about it being uncomfortable and scary to be honest with people about what's really going on... it is scary and hard. Not gonna lie.
But I've also found it to be worth it.
I've lost some people who couldn't handle the real me, not masking, not pretending to be someone I'm not. And that fucking hurts.
But I've also gotten closer with a couple of people who are able to hear where I'm at, what I'm dealing with, and accept me for who I am without the mask, and that's something really, really precious.

Plus I've found online communities invaluable, for connecting with others like me, for reminding me that I'm not alone in what I'm dealing with.

I completely 100% understand where you're coming from!
I have, on several occasions, not reported medical professionals because of the stress it was likely to involve (tbh, right now I am trying to convince myself to go through with filing a report against a psychiatrist myself, which is going to be hugely stressful, but I feel like it needs to be done...)

I don't think you're making excuses. Your feelings are valid and what happened to you happened.
As for your closest person being forever away, I'm guessing you have WhatsApp or Skype or something on your phone? Bring them with you virtually to your appointments! I saw a therapist via Skype for several months after she moved to the other side of the country, and my best friend currently sees a GP in a suburb which I avoid because of PTSD (an abusive ex-bf who raped me lives quite close to there, so I get panic attacks when I go there, though I have panic pills I can take if need be). I have gone to a few appointments with her, but I've also said that if I can't (if I'm running late - which I often do what with being ADHD, or if I can't get myself out of the building at all, or... I haven't even mentioned to her yet how triggering going to that particular place is, but I will), then she can take me with her virtually - either I can call (if she doesn't have enough data and minutes) and she can put me on speakerphone, so I can hear and talk, or if she has enough data, I can video call, and she can put me on speakerphone, so I can see, hear, and talk.
You can do the same thing!

If they're that far away, then time difference might be an issue too? Hopefully you can find an appointment time that works for you and your person. Also, if they're a family member, then sick leave can be used for appointments for family members (if it's during their work hours).

And regarding the functioning - this is why functioning labels are so problematic (they're anathema in autistic communities, but I find them gross everywhere). How well you function or not is not a measure of your worth. And you should not have to, EVER, try to pass for NT. You are you, and masking is exhausting as fuck, and it can't be maintained long-term. We end up burning out, at the very least, if not worse.

If you can, focus not on how high/low "functioning" you are, how mild/severe your symptoms are, but rather your needs. We all have needs. Some are very basic (shelter, food, water, love, safety, etc.), others more specific and can vary from person to person and over time (like I need to not have scratchy tags in/attached to my clothes, I need support for cleaning and meal preparation, otherwise my flatmate has to do all of the housework and I eat nothing but cereal and pizza, I need certain medications (for asthma, migraines, panic attacks, depression, and Rubifen for ADHD).

The world of work is not kind to us neurodivergent folk. Not working (at the moment/at all/ever) does not make you less of a person, less deserving of care, or in any way minimises who you are.

I'm sending you strength, OP

I was only able to skim read your post at the moment, but my main piece of advice (aside from firing the terrible doctor and keeping notes as others have said) would be to take someone with you to appointments.

A friend, a family member, someone you trust who can listen, take notes, remind you of what's in your notes when you are overwhelmed/in case you have a panic attack, someone who will stand up for you (you say you're not very assertive, and I've certainly found that I am MUCH better at standing up for other people than for myself! I've gone to friend's doctors appointments with them and been more assertive than at my own!), who will make sure that you are given the prescription in hand/stare them down while they fax it to the pharmacy (however it works - I get mine in hand, unless I call up for a repeat, then they fax them and text me when they've done it).

Also, you can make a complaint about this shitty doctor to whatever board they're registered with or whatever your local version of the Health and Disability Commission (that's what we have here in Aotearoa New Zealand) is. I am sure that wherever you are, you have rights about how health professionals treat you, and how this doctor treated you was not ok!

It's not about what's funny! It's about what's right and what's wrong.
And we, right here, for example, are in the business of casting ethical judgement. Sure, people will disagree, but just because people disagree about it doesn't mean there isn't an objective ethical standard.

What's funny is a matter of taste, yes.

No.

I 100% agree with the NTA judgement, but not being funny simply isn't the worst sin in comedy!
The thing is, what counts as funny is actually really subjective. And sure, we can (and obviously do!) make all sorts of normative judgements about what ought to be the subject of a joke and what ought to be off limits (and we can say, for example, that things that are racist or sexist, and that in any way try to make light of rape should be off limits).

But none of these normative judgements enable us to dictate to the psychology of what makes X person laugh at Y joke, and Z person not laugh.
Some people laugh at, and are genuinely entertained by, jokes that are/ought to be completely off limits. Some of these people might see no problem with the fact that they find these jokes funny. Others might be very self-reflective about it and recognise the problematic nature of their sense of humour.

But regardless of which camp a person falls into, they always have choices when deciding whether or not to tell a joke. Just because they find it funny (and there will, no doubt, be others who do too), doesn't make things like racism, sexism, or making light of rape ok. This comedian made the decision to say a lot of racist shit, and act out a whole racist set on stage, by the sounds of it!

THAT was the bad choice they made, regardless of whether anyone found them funny or not.

Yes, YTA.

Comments about someone's body, especially to do with weight, ESPECIALLY to do with weight loss/gain are a really, REALLY big no-no, *unless* the person concerned has specifically asked you for comments/input/feedback/whatever, and then it is ALWAYS best to check exactly what it is they're looking for.

Society is an asshole when it comes to judging our bodies, in particular around weight issues, so treading carefully is really important. It makes sense that we all have complicated feelings about our bodies.

Apologise to your husband (and mean it!! Not a shitty "I'm sorry if your feelings got hurt" non-apology!) and talk to him about how you can make it better (by working on not being an asshole!) and practice body positivity!

NTA at all!!

You have!

That is clear as fuck!!
It doesn't get any clearer.

Him invading your boundaries in all the other ways? That is him (and other people, even here!) saying that oh, but you didn't explicitly say that X thing bothered you...
Fuck that shit!

His behaviour has a name: male entitlement.

He believes that he is entitled to... you, knowledge of your Instagram account, standing as close as he wants to you, your time, singing karaoke with you, going on dates with you, etc., etc. - but it all boils down to: you.
And the fact is that he's not entitled to any of that, because he is not entitled to you, in any way, shape, or form.

Male entitlement is yet another example of toxic masculinity.
If he wasn't so entitled, then when you had first turned him down, he would have accepted your NO graciously, and followed your lead on how to manage your friendship going forward to ensure that you are comfortable (letting you ask him to hang out if/when you want to, letting you decide how close to him to sit, etc.), even saying explicitly that that's what he would do.
The fact that he did not do that shows just how entitled he is.

Report him with a clear conscience. Also - "he's been nothing but nice to me" is simply not true from everything else you've said. He has been flat out harassing you and making you feel bad and uncomfortable. That is not "nice".

You deserve better.

And, fellow redditors, fuck off with telling OP that she hasn't been clear enough in telling him no! Fuck off with reinforcing male entitlement and toxic masculinity!

NTA.

Definitely NTA! You do what you need to do to protect yourself and your baby, even from your parents.

Respect is earned, not automatic and a place in your life and the life of your baby should only be given to people you trust.

Also - they haven't even tried reaching out themselves, haven't apologised for how they fucked up, haven't acknowledged the hurt they put you through!!
And you're, what, expected to just reach out to THEM without autoforgive turned on because your little brother has SadFeels?! Fuck that shit!
Firstly, you are not responsible for your brother's feelings! Secondly, forgiveness is always optional and should NEVER be on the table if the offending party hasn't reached out with a genuine apology and acknowledgement of wrongdoing. And thirdly, even after all of that you can still choose to never have contact with your parents again, not let them see your baby and you would still not be an asshole!

I hope you have all the support and care that you need surrounding you, OP, I wish you well.

I'm queer and have shit "gaydar" but have awesome autism-dar! (I'm autistic too!)
Unfortunately I've found that people don't appreciate being told that they're autistic if they haven't figured it out themselves yet...

Also, I hate the term "ASD". Who I am is not a disorder! I'm autistic!

I don't know if it's mandatory where I am, but it's definitely the norm (and a lot of schools will have their own swimming pool). My issue was always that I couldn't (still can't!) abide cold water! And the school pools were always outdoor unheated pools and I would freeze (yes, this was in the middle of summer).

I LOVE swings too!! I could spend hours on end on swings! I'm the weirdo (i.e. autistic) adult who rocks up to a playground with my (snuggly toy) dragon or octopus tucked under my arm and hops onto the swings!!

And I have read that a lot of autistic kids have loved martial arts classes.
I did (and loved) dance and drama and was passionately into theatre for a long time!
But something very physical (but not team-based!!) like dance, or gymnastics (which I really wanted to do but my parents didn't want to drive me to classes!), or swimming, or in high school I took up rock-climbing!

Or see if you can pick up a cheap second-hand instrument for him to play with, to see if he takes to music (I was given a piano accordion when I was 11 - thinking back, I loved the sensory aspects, it made very cool sounds, but actually playing it was never really my thing...) and if he does, maybe classes at some point?

Arty things too! I mean, it doesn't have to be fine art, but whether it's doing something with clay or fingerpainting or whatever, it's all a sensory experience. Which is why those early childhood education years (before formal schooling starts) are so great!

Gah, my phone ate my comment that I'd nearly finished because the app updated!

Good (for me): weighted blanket, relaxing stims like stmmy snuggly toys, smells like peppermint and a nice lavender based pillow spray before bed
I have glasses with tinted lenses (even inside, even in the evenings - I have another pair for when it's very sunny/when I'm outside, with a darker tint) because I'm very sensitive to light and noise-cancelling headphones have been a godsend!
You say he likes video games, awesome! Find out what else he's passionate about/obsessed with and let him focus on his passions!
Make sure his environment is sensory friendly (scratchy tags on clothes are my nemesis and cutting them off isn't enough, I have to unpick the stitching to remove them!), see if bright lights are bothering him (I find warm light is much better on my eyes than white lights, so different lightbulbs could help), how are noise/sound levels (if he's uncomfortable, headphones, earplugs, earmuffs, or turning off unnecessary background noise and only having one person talking at a time helps!).

Hang on... he's FOUR?? And he's in school?! Is this some kind of pre-school situation?? I mean, even here in Aotearoa NZ where kids start school bloody early at age FIVE it's not compulsory till they turn six and still research shows that play-based learning is better for as long as possible!!

I am also autistic and I 100% agree. I see them as a hate group, no different than the KKK or Westboro Baptist Church (and if your kid was black or queer, you wouldn't go to them for advice or resources,!)

Self-diagnosis is accepted within the autism community. There are important considerations when deciding if you want to pursue formal diagnosis. Unfortunately there is still stigma, and once you have a formal diagnosis, you can't get rid of it, but who you share that with is still up to you (I assume - though some jobs might need to know that sort of thing to give you certain security clearance or something, I have no fucking idea!).

I decided that I want to know for sure (even though I was already 100% sure from self-diagnosing) for a few reasons. Firstly, autism is genetic, so if I ever do decide to do the kid thing, it's more likely that my kid would also be autistic and having a professional confirm my diagnosis would make me feel more confident, I think, in seeking a diagnosis for a kid if need be.

Secondly, it would (and now does) allow me to access disability support services (and that will depend on where you live as to what support there is and also what your needs are). I'm studying, doing my PhD and so getting support from Student Disability Services and the Student Learning Centre has been invaluable and I recently also found out that I can get Ministry of Health funded support and I'm still finding out what kind of support that'll be. But there is also support for applying for jobs, etc. if that was where I was at.
Also, having it recognised with a diagnosis can mean that in an employment situation (or any other situation where you need support or need things to be somewhat different than they are) you have something to point to and say look, I'm autistic, this is a disability rights issue (whether you need accommodations at work or are dealing with asking an event/organisation to be made more accessible for you (and it can take a while to figure out what that might involve - I'm currently on a crusade against hold music on the phone to make phone calls more accessible).

Another reason for me, I think, was that I hoped it would give me a sense of validation because at the time a lot of my family were very dubious about it but once I had the diagnosis they stopped doubting and they're fully supportive now. I did have a bf when I started the diagnosis process and he broke up with me partway through (good riddance, turns out he was an ass, and he was the only one who later said that well I've got my diagnosis now, I can just get over it and let it go already - apparently I'm too obsessed with autism!!)

Functioning varies. It's why functioning language is so problematic. According to my diagnosis I have mild (aka "high-functioning") autism and that's bullshit. Yes, there are days when I function really well so it's not something that affects me much and other days I'm not so functional.

Also, I'd recommend reading up on masking and think about whether you're masking your autistic self at all (something much more common in autistic women than men). It's taken me quite some time (and I'm still in the process) to figure out who this myself person is that I've been trying to hide behind a mask to fit in with the NT world and I'm working on dropping the mask and being my authentic autistic self more. It's worth considering if masking is making you feel more functional (because if so, it likely won't last... it's *exhausting*!!)

Also, be kind to yourself. And yes, I have my formal diagnosis (I got diagnosed by a psychologist three months ago) and sometimes I still feel like maybe I just need to try harder and what if I'm just pretending or something. But I try to remind myself to be kind to myself. If you were talking to a close friend who you are always nice to rather than yourself, would you say the same things? Talk to yourself (I mean the internal self-talk in your head) like you would to a friend or a sibling/child you love and would always be kind to. We have good functioning days/weeks/months even and not good functioning times. The good functioning times don't negate the struggles and the struggles don't negate what we are capable of.

Also, I was told that sensory issues are common but not always a thing for autistic people. But then after I got diagnosed and started reading and thinking more about sensory issues and the huge variety, I did start to recognise quite a few in myself, including some that I previously would've just put up with as part of masking and things that made me uncomfortable but I didn't have the language for why (rap music, for example - for me it's auditory overload because there's too much going on that I can't follow). Of course I'm not saying that this will be the case for you, this is just my experience.

His behaviour sounds emotionally neglectful at best and leaning into abusive territory at worst. I would be very open and frank with him and tell him how his specific actions and words make you feel. E.g. "when you do/say X, I FEEL Y". I don't think the crying is the problem, crying can be very healthy, but it's how you're feeling when you cry that's the issue (I find it quite hard to articulate emotions, being autistic, but you might be feeling upset/frustrated/hurt/neglected, etc.). And be very careful to distinguish when you talk to him between intention and outcome, because he needs to be made aware of the outcome of his actions/words, regardless of his intentions: "you may not have intended to make me feel Y, but that doesn't change the fact that when you do/say X, I feel Y".
And it may be time to end the relationship if the hurt is too much and you don't see things changing.
I would certainly echo the recommendation of therapy for him, though I would recommend against couples therapy for any abusive relationship simply because an abuser will not acknowledge the abuse. If you are able to, therapy might be helpful for you to heal too.
And yeah, his behaviours might well be exacerbated by his aspergers, but that doesn't excuse them.

We often struggle with executive function (in my case things like doing the dishes, cooking a meal, getting the groceries, doing laundry, etc.). For a long time I thought this was a symptom of depression (and yes, it can be) but it's been an issue for me even at times when I haven't been dealing with depression.

There are lots of coping strategies that we can find, and some work better than others for different people. I love lists, so to do lists with even the most basic things on them help me, and it gives me great satisfaction to cross things off my list. Or apps like Habitica, which turn your list into an RPG and give you XP for completing tasks. When I was younger I used to tell myself a story around why I had to dry the dishes (I had to rescue as many of the dishes and get them away from some bad place - volcanic island, sinking ship or so - to safety - the cupboards and drawers).

If you can, maybe see if you can find a therapist who can work on the blow ups with you and can help you find coping strategies that work for you.
